The wolf ran forward and jumped heavily over a gully in its path. It was an old animal with a gray back and a big reddish belly. It ran without haste, clearly confident no one had spotted it. Rostov, holding his breath, glanced at the borzois. They stood or lay there, not seeing the wolf, not grasping the situation. Old Karay had turned his head and was angrily snapping at fleas, baring his yellow teeth and nipping at his hind legs.

"Ulyulyulyu!" Rostov whispered, pursing his lips. The borzois jumped up, jerking their leash-rings and pricking their ears. Karay finished scratching, cocked his ears, and stood up with quivering tail, tufts of matted hair hanging from his thigh.

"Should I release them or not?" Nicholas asked himself as the wolf approached from the copse. Suddenly the wolf's whole expression changed: it shuddered, seeing what it had probably never seen before — human eyes fixed upon it — and, turning its head slightly toward Rostov, it paused.
"Forward or back? No matter — forward..." the wolf seemed to decide, and it moved on without another backward glance, in a quiet, long, easy but resolute lope.

"Ulyulyu!" cried Nicholas in a voice not his own, and of its own accord his good horse plunged headlong downhill, leaping over gullies to cut off the wolf, and the borzois raced past even faster. Nicholas didn't hear his own shout, didn't feel himself galloping, didn't see the borzois or the ground beneath him — he saw only the wolf, which quickened its pace and bounded in the same direction along the hollow. The first to come into view was Milka, with her black markings and powerful hindquarters, gaining on the wolf. Closer and closer... now she was alongside. But the wolf turned its head to face her, and instead of putting on speed as she usually did, Milka suddenly raised her tail and braced her front legs.
"Ulyulyulyulyu!" shouted Nicholas.

The reddish Lyubim rushed forward from behind Milka, sprang boldly at the wolf, and seized it by the haunches — but instantly jumped away in terror. The wolf crouched, snapped its jaws, and rose again, bounding forward. All the borzois followed at a distance of a couple of feet but couldn't close the gap.
"She'll get away! No, it's impossible!" thought Nicholas, still shouting in a hoarse voice.

"Karay, ulyulyu!" he called, looking around for the old borzoi who was now his only hope. Karay, with all the strength his age still allowed, stretched himself to the utmost and, watching the wolf, galloped heavily at an angle to cut it off. But the wolf's speed and the borzoi's slower pace made it clear that Karay had misjudged the angle. Nicholas could already see the woods not far ahead — the wolf would certainly escape if it reached them. But coming toward him from that direction he saw hounds and a huntsman galloping almost straight at the wolf. There was still hope. A long, yellowish young borzoi that Nicholas didn't recognize — from another leash — rushed at the wolf from the front and nearly knocked it over. But the wolf recovered faster than anyone could have expected and, snapping its jaws, flew at the yellowish borzoi, which fell with a piercing yelp, its head hitting the ground, blood pouring from a gash in its side.
"Karay! Old boy!..." wailed Nicholas.

Thanks to the delay caused by the young borzoi's charge, old Karay, with his matted hair hanging from his thigh, had closed to within five paces. As if sensing its danger, the wolf glanced at Karay, tucked its tail even tighter between its legs, and ran faster. But at that moment Nicholas saw something happen to Karay — the borzoi was suddenly on top of the wolf, and together they tumbled into a gully just ahead.

That instant — when Nicholas saw the wolf struggling in the gully with the dogs while from beneath them he could make out its gray fur and outstretched hind leg and its frightened, choking head with ears laid back, Karay pinning it by the throat — was the happiest moment of his life. With his hand on the saddlebow, he was ready to dismount and stab the wolf when it suddenly thrust its head up from the mass of dogs and got its front paws onto the edge of the gully. It clicked its teeth — Karay no longer had it by the throat — and with a movement of its hind legs leaped out of the gully. Having shaken off the dogs, it tucked its tail in again and loped forward. Karay, his fur bristling and probably bruised or hurt, climbed with difficulty out of the gully.
"Oh my God! Why?" Nicholas cried in despair.
"Uncle's" huntsman was galloping from the other side to block the wolf's path, and his borzois once more stopped its advance. It was hemmed in again.

Nicholas, his attendant, "Uncle," and his huntsman were all riding around the wolf, shouting "ulyulyu!" and preparing to dismount each time the wolf crouched back, then surging forward again each time it shook itself free and headed for the wood where it would be safe.

Already at the beginning of the chase, Daniel — hearing the ulyulyuing — had burst out of the wood. He had seen Karay seize the wolf and checked his horse, thinking the business was over. But when he saw that the horsemen weren't dismounting and the wolf had shaken itself free and was heading for safety, Daniel set his chestnut galloping — not toward the wolf, but straight for the wood, to cut it off, just as Karay had tried to do. Thanks to this he galloped up to the wolf just as it was being stopped a second time by "Uncle's" borzois.
Daniel rode up in silence, holding a naked dagger in his left hand and lashing the laboring sides of his chestnut horse with his whip as if it were a flail.

Nicholas neither saw nor heard Daniel until the chestnut, breathing heavily, panted past him, and he heard the thud of a body falling and saw Daniel lying on the wolf's back among the dogs, trying to seize it by the ears. It was clear to the dogs, the hunters, and to the wolf itself that all was now over. The terrified wolf pressed back its ears and tried to rise, but the borzois clung to it. Daniel got up slightly, took a step, and with his whole weight — as if lying down to rest — threw himself on the wolf, seizing it by the ears. Nicholas was about to stab it, but Daniel whispered: "Don't! We'll muzzle it!" Shifting his position, he planted his foot on the wolf's neck. A stick was thrust between its jaws and it was tied up with a leash, like a bridle; its legs were bound together, and Daniel rolled it over once or twice.

With happy, exhausted faces they loaded the live old wolf onto a rearing, snorting horse and, accompanied by dogs yelping at it, carried it to the meeting place. The hounds had killed two of the cubs and the borzois three. The huntsmen gathered with their trophies and their stories, and everyone came to look at the wolf, which, with its broad-browed head hanging down and the bitten stick clamped between its jaws, stared with large, glassy eyes at the crowd of dogs and men surrounding it. When someone touched it, it jerked its bound legs and looked at them all with a wild yet simple gaze. Old Count Rostov rode up too and touched the wolf.
"Oh, what a brute!" he said. "A real brute, eh?" he asked Daniel, who was standing nearby.
"Yes, your excellency," answered Daniel, quickly doffing his cap.
The count remembered the wolf he had let slip and his encounter with Daniel.
"Ah, but you are a crusty fellow, friend!" said the count.
For his only reply, Daniel gave him a shy, childlike, meek, and endearing smile.

title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: The old count went home, and Natasha and Petya promised to return very soon, but since it was still early the hunt continued. At midday they put the hounds into a ravine thickly overgrown with young trees. Nicholas, standing in a fallow field, could see all his whips.

Facing him lay a field of winter rye; there his own huntsman stood alone in a hollow behind a hazel bush. The hounds had barely been released before Nicholas heard a familiar hound, Voltorn, giving tongue at intervals; others joined in, now pausing and now sounding again. A moment later a cry came from the wooded ravine that a fox had been found, and the whole pack, joining together, raced along the ravine toward the rye field and away from Nicholas.
He could see the whips in their red caps galloping along the edge of the ravine; he even caught sight of the hounds, and was expecting a fox to appear any moment on the rye field opposite.

The huntsman in the hollow moved and released his borzois, and Nicholas saw a strange, short-legged red fox with a fine brush running hard across the field. The borzois bore down on it... They drew close to the fox, which started dodging in tighter and tighter curves, trailing its brush — when suddenly a strange white borzoi dashed in, followed by a black one, and everything was confusion. The borzois formed a star-shaped cluster, barely swaying their bodies and with tails pointing away from the center. Two huntsmen galloped up to the dogs — one in a red cap, the other, a stranger, in a green coat.
"What's going on?" thought Nicholas. "Where did that huntsman come from? He's not one of Uncle's men."

The huntsmen secured the fox but stayed there for a long time without tying it to the saddle. Their horses, bridled and with high saddles, stood nearby, and the dogs lay on the ground. The huntsmen were waving their arms and doing something with the fox. Then from that spot came the blast of a horn — the signal agreed upon in case of a fight.
"That's Ilagin's huntsman having a row with our Ivan," said Nicholas's groom.
Nicholas sent the man to call Natasha and Petya and rode at a walk toward where the whips were gathering the hounds. Several riders from the field galloped toward the spot of the fight.

Nicholas dismounted, and with Natasha and Petya, who had ridden up, stood near the hounds, waiting to see how the matter would end. Out of the bushes rode the huntsman who had been fighting, heading for his young master with the fox tied to his crupper. While still some distance away he took off his cap and tried to speak respectfully, but his face was pale and he was breathing hard, and his expression was furious. One eye was black, though he probably didn't even realize it.
"What happened?" asked Nicholas.

"A likely story — killing a fox our dogs had hunted! And it was my gray bitch that caught it! Go to court if you like!... He grabs at the fox! I gave him one with the fox across the face. Here it is, on my saddle! Want a taste of this?" said the huntsman, pointing to his dagger, probably imagining he was still talking to his enemy.
Nicholas, without stopping to hear more, asked his sister and Petya to wait for him and rode toward the place where the rival — Ilagin's — hunting party was.
The victorious huntsman rode off to join the field and there, surrounded by curious well-wishers, recounted his exploits.

The facts were that Ilagin — with whom the Rostovs had a quarrel and were in litigation — hunted over lands that belonged by custom to the Rostovs, and had now, as if deliberately, sent his men to the very woods the Rostovs were hunting and let his huntsman snatch a fox their dogs had chased.

Nicholas, though he had never met Ilagin, with his usual lack of moderation in passing judgment, hated him with all his heart based on reports of his high-handedness and violence, and regarded him as his worst enemy. He rode toward him in furious agitation, gripping his whip, fully prepared to take the most extreme and desperate action to punish his foe.
He had barely passed the corner of the wood when a stout gentleman in a beaver cap came riding toward him on a handsome raven-black horse, accompanied by two hunt servants.

Instead of the enemy he expected, Nicholas found in Ilagin a dignified and courteous gentleman who was especially eager to make the young count's acquaintance. Riding up, Ilagin raised his beaver cap and said he deeply regretted what had happened and would punish the man who had allowed himself to seize a fox hunted by someone else's borzois. He expressed his hope of becoming better acquainted with the count and invited him to hunt his own covert.

Natasha, who had been afraid her brother would do something terrible, had followed him nervously. Seeing the two enemies exchanging friendly greetings, she rode up to them. Ilagin raised his beaver cap even higher to Natasha and said, with a pleasant smile, that the young countess reminded him of Diana, both in her passion for the hunt and in her beauty, of which he had heard much.

To atone for his huntsman's offense, Ilagin urged the Rostovs to come to a stretch of upland about a mile away that he usually kept for himself and which, he said, was teeming with hares. Nicholas agreed, and the hunt, now doubled in size, moved on.

The way to Ilagin's ground led across open fields. The hunt servants fell into line. The masters rode together. "Uncle," Rostov, and Ilagin kept stealing glances at one another's dogs, trying not to be noticed by their companions, and anxiously searching for rivals to their own borzois.

Rostov was particularly struck by the beauty of a small, purebred, red-spotted bitch on Ilagin's leash — slender, but with muscles like steel, a delicate muzzle, and prominent black eyes. He had heard of the speed of Ilagin's borzois, and in that beautiful bitch he saw a rival to his own Milka.
In the middle of a serious conversation about the year's harvest, Nicholas pointed to the red-spotted bitch.
"A fine little bitch, that!" he said casually. "Is she fast?"

"That one? Yes, she's a good dog — catches what she's after," answered Ilagin offhandedly, speaking of the bitch Erza, for which he had paid a neighbor three families of house serfs the year before. "So in your area too the harvest is nothing to boast about, Count?" he went on, continuing their earlier conversation. And thinking it polite to return the young count's compliment, Ilagin looked over his borzois and picked out Milka, which caught his eye with her powerful build. "That black-spotted one of yours is nice — well shaped!" he said.

"Yes, she's fast enough," replied Nicholas, and thought: "If only a full-grown hare would cross the field right now, I'd show you what kind of borzoi she is." Turning to his groom, he said he'd give a ruble to anyone who flushed a hare.

"I don't understand," continued Ilagin, "how some sportsmen can get so jealous about game and dogs. Personally, I can tell you, Count, I enjoy riding in company like this — what could be better?" He again raised his cap to Natasha. "But as for counting skins and keeping score, I don't care about any of that."
"Of course not!"
"Or getting upset because someone else's borzoi, not mine, catches something. All I care about is enjoying the chase — isn't that right, Count? Because I think that..."

"A-tu!" came the long-drawn cry of one of the borzoi whippers-in, who had stopped on a rise in the stubble. He stood on a hillock, holding his whip aloft, and again drew out his cry: "A-tu!" This call and the raised whip meant he had spotted a sitting hare.

"Ah, I think he's found one," said Ilagin casually. "Yes, let's ride up... Shall we both course it?" replied Nicholas, seeing in Erza and in "Uncle's" red Rugay two rivals he had never before had the chance to pit against his own borzois. "What if they outrun my Milka right away!" he thought as he rode with "Uncle" and Ilagin toward the hare.
"A full-grown one?" asked Ilagin as he approached the whip who had sighted the hare — and not without excitement he glanced around and whistled to Erza.
"And you, Michael Nikanorych?" he said, addressing "Uncle."
"Uncle" was riding with a grim expression.
"How can I compete? Why, you've paid a fortune for each of your borzois! That's it — come on! Yours are worth thousands. You two match your dogs against each other — I'll just watch!"

"Rugay, hey, hey!" he shouted. "Rugayushka!" he added, involuntarily using the diminutive to express his affection and the hopes he placed on this red borzoi. Natasha could see and feel the excitement the two older men and her brother were trying to hide, and was caught up in it herself.

The huntsman stood halfway up the hillock with his whip raised; the gentlemen rode up at a walk. The hounds far off on the horizon turned away from the hare, and the whips, but not the gentlemen, also moved aside. Everyone was moving slowly and deliberately.
"Which way is it pointing?" asked Nicholas, riding a hundred paces toward the whip.

But before the whip could answer, the hare — sensing the frost that was coming the next morning — could no longer sit still and leaped up. The pack on leash surged downhill in full cry after the hare, and from all directions the unleashed borzois charged after the hounds and the hare. All the hunters who had been moving slowly now shouted "Stop!" calling back the hounds, while the borzoi whippers-in galloped across the field with a cry of "A-tu!" setting the borzois loose. The composed Ilagin, Nicholas, Natasha, and "Uncle" flew forward, caring nothing for where or how they went, seeing only the borzois and the hare, and terrified of losing sight of the chase for even an instant. The hare they had started was a strong and swift one. When it jumped up it didn't bolt immediately but pricked its ears, listening to the shouts and pounding hooves from every side. It took a dozen bounds, not very fast, letting the borzois gain — and then, having chosen its direction and grasped the danger, laid back its ears and shot off at top speed. It had been lying in the stubble, but ahead of it was the autumn planting where the ground was soft. The two borzois of the huntsman who had spotted it, being closest, were first to see and pursue it, but they hadn't gone far before Ilagin's red-spotted Erza passed them, closed to within a length, and flew at the hare with terrifying speed, aiming at its tail — and, thinking she had seized it, tumbled head over heels like a ball. The hare arched its back and bounded off even faster. From behind, the broad-haunched, black-spotted Milka came rapidly gaining.

"Milashka, darling!" rose Nicholas's triumphant shout. It looked as if Milka would pounce on the hare any second, but she overtook it and shot past. The hare had squatted. Again the beautiful Erza caught up, but when close to the hare's tail she hesitated — as if measuring the distance, so as not to make the same mistake twice — and tried to seize its hind leg.

"Erza, darling!" Ilagin wailed in a voice unlike his own. Erza didn't listen. At the very instant she would have caught her prey, the hare swerved and darted along the boundary strip between the winter rye and the stubble. Again Erza and Milka ran neck and neck, like a pair of carriage horses, and started to overtake the hare. But it was easier for the hare to run on the strip, and the borzois didn't gain as quickly.

"Rugay, Rugayushka! That's it — come on!" came a third voice just then, and "Uncle's" red borzoi, straining and arching its back, caught up with the two leaders, pushed past them both, put on a burst of savage speed close to the hare, knocked it off the strip onto the rye field, surged forward even more ferociously — sinking to its knees in the muddy ground — and all one could see was how, covered in mud, it rolled over with the hare. A ring of borzois gathered around. A moment later everyone had ridden up. Only the elated "Uncle" dismounted and cut off a paw, shaking the hare so the blood dripped off, glancing around with restless eyes while his arms and legs twitched. He spoke without knowing whom he was addressing or what he was saying. "That's it — come on! There's a dog for you!... Beat them all — the thousand-ruble ones and the one-ruble ones alike. That's it — come on!" he said, panting, looking around furiously as if they were all his enemies who had insulted him, and only now had he at last vindicated himself. "There go your thousand-ruble borzois... That's it — come on!"
"Rugay, here's a paw for you!" he said, tossing down the hare's muddy foot. "You earned it — that's it — come on!"
"She'd tired herself out — she'd run it down three times on her own," said Nicholas, also not listening to anyone and not caring whether he was heard.
"But what's the trick in running across it like that?" said Ilagin's groom.

"Once she'd missed it and turned it away, any mutt could have caught it," Ilagin was saying at the same time, breathless from the gallop and the excitement. At that same moment Natasha, without stopping to breathe, let out a shriek — so joyous, so ecstatic, and so piercing that it set everyone's ears ringing. With that shriek she expressed what all the others were expressing by talking at once, and it was so wild that she herself would normally have been mortified by it, and everyone else would have been astonished at any other time. "Uncle" himself tucked the hare neatly and smartly across his horse's back — as if rebuking everyone with the gesture — and, with an air of not wanting to speak to anyone, mounted his bay and rode away. All the others followed, deflated and shamefaced, and only much later were they able to resume their former pretense of indifference. For a long time they kept looking at the red Rugay, who trotted along behind "Uncle's" horse with his arched, mud-spattered back and the ring of his leash clanking — walking with the serene air of a conqueror.
"Well, I'm like any other dog when it's not a matter of coursing. But when it is — watch out!" his appearance seemed to say to Nicholas.
When, much later, "Uncle" rode up to Nicholas and began to talk, he felt flattered that after what had happened "Uncle" condescended to speak to him.

title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: Toward evening Ilagin took his leave of Nicholas, who found that they were so far from home that he accepted "Uncle's" offer for the hunting party to spend the night at his little village of Mikhaylovna.
"And if you stay at my house, that's even better. That's it — come on!" said "Uncle." "You see it's damp weather, and you could rest, and the little countess could be driven home in a cart."
"Uncle's" offer was accepted. A huntsman was sent to Otradnoe for a cart, while Nicholas rode with Natasha and Petya to "Uncle's" house.

About five male household serfs, big and small, rushed out to the front porch to greet their master. A score of women serfs, old and young, along with children, peeked out from the back entrance to get a look at the hunters arriving. The sight of Natasha — a woman, a lady, on horseback — raised their curiosity to such a pitch that many of them walked right up to her, stared into her face, and, completely unfazed by her presence, made remarks about her as though she were some exotic creature on display and not a human being who could hear and understand what was being said.
"Arinka! Look, she rides sideways! There she sits and her skirt hangs down... See, she's got a little hunting horn!"
"Goodness gracious! Look at her knife!..."
"She must be a Tartar!"
"How come you didn't fall off?" asked the boldest of them all, addressing Natasha directly.

"Uncle" dismounted at the porch of his little wooden house, which stood in the middle of an overgrown garden, and after a glance at his servants shouted authoritatively for the unnecessary ones to clear off and for all the proper preparations to be made for the guests.

The servants all scattered. "Uncle" lifted Natasha off her horse, took her hand, and led her up the rickety wooden steps. The house, with its bare, unplastered log walls, was not especially clean — no one living there seemed to aim for spotlessness — but neither was it noticeably neglected. In the entryway there was a smell of fresh apples, and wolf and fox skins hung on the walls.

"Uncle" led the visitors through the front hall into a small room with a folding table and red chairs, then into the drawing room with its round birchwood table and sofa, and finally into his private study, where there was a worn sofa, a threadbare carpet, and portraits of Suvorov, of the host's father and mother, and of himself in military uniform. The study smelled strongly of tobacco and dogs. "Uncle" asked his guests to sit down and make themselves at home, and then went out. Rugay, his back still muddy, came into the room and lay on the sofa, cleaning himself with his tongue and teeth. Leading from the study was a passage with a partition hung with ragged curtains. From behind this came women's laughter and whispers. Natasha, Nicholas, and Petya took off their outdoor things and sat down on the sofa. Petya, leaning on his elbow, fell asleep at once. Natasha and Nicholas were silent. Their faces glowed, they were hungry and very cheerful. They looked at each other — now that the hunt was over and they were indoors, Nicholas no longer saw any need to demonstrate his manly superiority over his sister — Natasha winked at him, and neither of them could hold back a burst of ringing laughter even before they had a reason for it.

After a while "Uncle" came in wearing a Cossack coat, blue trousers, and short boots. Natasha realized that this outfit — the very one she had viewed with surprise and amusement at Otradnoe — was exactly right and not at all inferior to a tailcoat or frock coat. "Uncle" too was in high spirits and far from taking offense at the brother's and sister's laughter — it would never enter his mind that they might be laughing at his way of life — he joined right in.

"That's right, little countess — that's it, come on! I've never seen anyone like her!" he said, offering Nicholas a long-stemmed pipe and, with a practiced motion of three fingers, taking down another that had been cut short. "She's ridden all day like a man, and she's as fresh as ever!"

Soon after "Uncle's" reappearance, the door opened — evidently by a barefoot girl, judging by the sound — and a stout, rosy, good-looking woman of about forty entered, carrying a large loaded tray. She had a double chin and full red lips. With hospitable dignity and warmth in her gaze and in every movement, she looked at the guests and, with a pleasant smile, bowed respectfully. Despite her considerable stoutness — which made her chest and stomach protrude and her head tilt back — she moved with remarkable lightness. She went to the table, set down the tray, and with plump white hands deftly arranged the bottles, appetizers, and dishes. When she finished she stepped aside and stood by the door with a smile. "Here I am. This is me! Now do you understand Uncle?" her expression said to Rostov. How could one not understand? Not only Nicholas but even Natasha grasped the meaning of his puckered brow and the happy, self-satisfied smile that slightly creased his lips when Anisya Fedorovna entered. On the tray was a bottle of herb wine, various vodkas, pickled mushrooms, rye cakes made with buttermilk, honeycomb, still mead and sparkling mead, apples, nuts — raw and roasted — and nut-and-honey sweets. Then she brought a freshly roasted chicken, ham, preserves made with honey, and preserves made with sugar.

All of this was the fruit of Anisya Fedorovna's housekeeping, gathered and prepared by her. The smell and taste of everything carried a trace of Anisya Fedorovna herself: a flavor of juiciness, cleanliness, freshness, and pleasant smiles.
"Try this, little Lady-Countess!" she kept saying, offering Natasha first one thing and then another.
Natasha ate everything and thought she had never seen or tasted such buttermilk cakes, such fragrant jam, such honey-and-nut sweets, or such a chicken anywhere. Anisya Fedorovna left the room.

After supper, over their cherry brandy, Rostov and "Uncle" talked about past and future hunts, about Rugay and Ilagin's dogs, while Natasha sat upright on the sofa listening with sparkling eyes. She tried several times to wake Petya so he could eat something, but he only mumbled incoherent words without waking up. Natasha felt so lighthearted and happy in these unfamiliar surroundings that she dreaded the cart coming for her too soon. After one of those pauses that often occur when hosting friends for the first time, "Uncle" — responding to a thought that was in his guests' minds — said:
"This, you see, is how I'm finishing my days... Death will come. That's it — come on! Nothing will be left. So why do harm to anyone?"

"Uncle's" face was very striking and even handsome as he said this. Nicholas couldn't help recalling all the good things he had heard about him from his father and the neighbors. Throughout the whole province "Uncle" had a reputation as the most honest and selfless of eccentrics. People called him in to settle family disputes, chose him as executor of wills, entrusted him with secrets, elected him as justice and to other positions; but he always stubbornly refused public office, spending autumn and spring in the fields on his bay gelding, sitting at home in winter, and lying in his overgrown garden in summer.
"Why don't you enter the service, Uncle?"

"I did once, but gave it up. I'm not cut out for it. That's it — come on! I can't make head or tail of it. That's for you — I haven't got the brains. Now, hunting is another matter — that's it — come on! Open the door there!" he shouted. "Why have you shut it?"
The door at the end of the passage led to the huntsmen's room, as the servants' quarters for the hunt were called.

There was a quick patter of bare feet, and an unseen hand opened the door to the huntsmen's room, from which came the clear sounds of a balalaika played by someone who was obviously a master of the instrument. Natasha had been listening to those strains for some time and now went out into the passage to hear better.
"That's Mitka, my coachman... I got him a good balalaika. I'm fond of it," said "Uncle."
It was the custom for Mitka to play the balalaika in the huntsmen's room when "Uncle" returned from the hunt. "Uncle" loved this kind of music.
"How good! Really very good!" said Nicholas, with some unintentional condescension, as if embarrassed to admit how much the sounds pleased him.
"Very good?" said Natasha reproachfully, catching her brother's tone. "Not 'very good' — it's simply wonderful!"
Just as "Uncle's" pickled mushrooms, honey, and cherry brandy had seemed to her the best in the world, so also that music, at that moment, seemed the pinnacle of musical beauty.

"More, please, more!" cried Natasha from the doorway as soon as the balalaika stopped. Mitka tuned up again and began strumming the melody of My Lady, with trills and variations. "Uncle" sat listening with a slight smile, his head tilted to one side. The tune was repeated a hundred times. The balalaika was retuned several times and the same notes thrummed again, but the listeners never tired of it and only wished to hear it over and over. Anisya Fedorovna came in and leaned her ample figure against the doorpost.
"You like listening?" she said to Natasha, with a smile exactly like "Uncle's." "He plays well, our man," she added.
"He's not playing that part right!" said "Uncle" suddenly, with an emphatic gesture. "Here he should burst out — that's it — come on! — he should burst out."
"Do you play?" asked Natasha.
"Uncle" didn't answer, but smiled.
"Anisya, go check if the strings on my guitar are in order. I haven't touched it in a long time. That's it — come on! I've given it up."
Anisya Fedorovna, with her light step, went willingly to carry out the errand and brought back the guitar.

Without looking at anyone, "Uncle" blew the dust off it, tapped the case with his bony fingers, tuned the guitar, and settled himself in his armchair. He took the guitar a little above the fingerboard, arching his left elbow with a somewhat theatrical gesture, and — with a wink at Anisya Fedorovna — struck a single chord, pure and resonant. Then, quietly, smoothly, and confidently, he began playing in very slow time — not My Lady, but the well-known folk song: Came a maiden down the street. The tune, played with precision and in perfect time, began to thrill in the hearts of Nicholas and Natasha, awakening in them the same kind of sober joy that radiated from Anisya Fedorovna's whole being. Anisya Fedorovna blushed, drew her kerchief over her face, and went laughing out of the room. "Uncle" continued to play correctly, carefully, with firm resolve, gazing with a changed, inspired expression at the spot where Anisya Fedorovna had just stood. Something seemed to be smiling on one side of his face beneath his gray mustache, especially as the song grew brisker and the tempo quicker, and when — here and there, as he ran his fingers over the strings — something seemed to snap.

"Lovely, lovely! Go on, Uncle, go on!" shouted Natasha as soon as he finished. She jumped up and hugged and kissed him. "Nicholas, Nicholas!" she said, turning to her brother, as if asking him: "What is this that moves me so?"
Nicholas too was very pleased by "Uncle's" playing, and "Uncle" played the piece again. Anisya Fedorovna's smiling face reappeared in the doorway, and behind hers, other faces...
Fetching water clear and sweet, Stop, dear maiden, I entreat —
played "Uncle" once more, running his fingers skillfully over the strings, and then he stopped short and jerked his shoulders.
"Go on, Uncle dear," Natasha pleaded, as if her life depended on it.
"Uncle" rose, and it was as if there were two men in him: one smiled seriously at the other, the merry fellow, who struck a naive and precise pose preparatory to a folk dance.
"Now then, niece!" he exclaimed, waving to Natasha the hand that had just struck a chord.
Natasha threw off the shawl from her shoulders, ran forward to face "Uncle," and — setting her arms akimbo — also made a motion with her shoulders and struck a pose.

Where, how, and when had this young countess, educated by a French emigree governess, absorbed from the Russian air she breathed that spirit and manner which the shawl dance should, one would have thought, long ago have driven out of her? But the spirit and the movements were those inimitable, unteachable Russian ones that "Uncle" had expected of her. The instant she struck her pose and smiled triumphantly, proudly, and with sly merriment, the fear that had seized Nicholas and the others — that she might not do it right — vanished, and they were already admiring her.
* The French shawl dance.

She did it with such precision, such complete precision, that Anisya Fedorovna, who had immediately handed her the handkerchief she needed for the dance, had tears in her eyes as she watched, though she was laughing — watching this slim, graceful countess, raised in silks and velvets and so different from herself, who nevertheless understood everything that was in Anisya and in Anisya's father and mother and aunt, and in every Russian man and woman.

"Well, little countess — that's it — come on!" cried "Uncle" with a joyous laugh, having finished the dance. "Well done, niece! Now we need to find a fine young man for your husband. That's it — come on!"
"He's already been chosen," said Nicholas, smiling.
"Oh?" said "Uncle" in surprise, looking inquiringly at Natasha, who nodded with a happy smile.

"And such a one!" she said. But the moment she said it, a new train of thoughts and feelings arose in her. "What did Nicholas's smile mean when he said 'already chosen'? Is he glad or not? It's as if he thinks my Bolkonsky wouldn't approve of or understand our fun here. But he would understand it all. Where is he right now?" she wondered, and her face suddenly grew serious. But this lasted only a second. "Don't dare think about it," she told herself, and sat down again, smiling, beside "Uncle," asking him to play something more.
"Uncle" played another song and a waltz; then after a pause he cleared his throat and sang his favorite hunting song:
As 'twas growing dark last night, fell the snow so soft and light...

"Uncle" sang the way peasants sing, with the full, naive conviction that the whole meaning of a song lies in the words and that the tune comes by itself — that apart from the words there is no tune, which exists only to give rhythm to the words. As a result, the unstudied melody, like the song of a bird, was extraordinarily beautiful. Natasha was in ecstasies over "Uncle's" singing. She resolved to give up the harp and play only the guitar. She asked "Uncle" for his guitar and at once found the chords of the song.

After nine o'clock two carts and three mounted men, sent out to look for them, arrived to fetch Natasha and Petya. The count and countess had no idea where they were and were very worried, said one of the men.

Petya was carried out like a log and laid in the larger of the two carts. Natasha and Nicholas got into the other. "Uncle" wrapped Natasha up warmly and said goodbye with a quite new tenderness. He walked with them as far as the bridge, which couldn't be crossed, so they had to go around by the ford. He sent huntsmen ahead with lanterns.
"Goodbye, dear niece," his voice called from the darkness — not the voice Natasha had known before, but the one that had sung As 'twas growing dark last night.
In the village they were passing through there were red lights and a cheerful smell of wood smoke.
"What a darling Uncle is!" said Natasha, when they had come out onto the main road.
"Yes," said Nicholas. "You're not cold?"

"No, I'm completely, completely fine. I feel so comfortable!" answered Natasha, almost puzzled by her own contentment. They were silent for a long time. The night was dark and damp. They couldn't see the horses, only heard them splashing through the invisible mud.

What was happening in that receptive, childlike soul that so eagerly caught and absorbed all of life's varied impressions? How did they all find room in her? But she was very happy. As they neared home she suddenly began to sing As 'twas growing dark last night — the tune she had been trying to get the whole way and had finally caught.
"Got it?" said Nicholas.
"What were you thinking about just now, Nicholas?" asked Natasha.
They were fond of asking each other that question.

"Me?" said Nicholas, trying to remember. "Well, first I thought that Rugay, the red hound, was like Uncle — and that if he were a man he'd always keep Uncle near him, if not for his riding then for his personality. What a good fellow Uncle is! Don't you think? Well, and you?"

"Me? Wait a bit, wait... Yes, first I thought that we're driving along and imagining we're going home, but heaven knows where we're really going in the darkness, and that we'll arrive and suddenly find we're not in Otradnoe at all, but in fairyland. And then I thought... No, nothing else."
"I know — I bet you were thinking about him," said Nicholas, smiling, as Natasha could tell by the sound of his voice.

"No," said Natasha, though in fact she had been thinking about Prince Andrew along with everything else, and about how he would have liked "Uncle." "And then I kept saying to myself the whole way: 'How beautifully Anisya carried herself, how beautifully!'" And Nicholas heard her spontaneous, happy, ringing laughter. "And you know," she said suddenly, "I know that I will never again be as happy and at peace as I am right now."

"That's rubbish, nonsense, humbug!" exclaimed Nicholas, and thought: "How charming this Natasha of mine is! I have no other friend like her and never shall. Why does she have to marry? We could always drive about together like this!"
"What a darling this Nicholas of mine is!" thought Natasha.
"Ah, there are still lights in the drawing room!" she said, pointing to the windows of the house that gleamed invitingly in the moist, velvety darkness of the night.

title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: Count Ilya Rostov had given up the position of Provincial Marshal of the Nobility because it cost too much, but their finances had not improved. Natasha and Nicholas often noticed their parents conferring anxiously in private and heard talk of selling the grand ancestral Rostov house and the estate near Moscow. It was no longer necessary to entertain as lavishly as when the count had been Marshal, and life at Otradnoe was quieter than before — but still the enormous house and its wings were full of people, and more than twenty sat down to dinner every day. These were all people who had settled into the house almost as family members, or who seemed, for one reason or another, compelled to live in the count's household. There were Dimmler the musician and his wife, Vogel the dancing master and his family, Belova the elderly spinster who was an established member of the house, and many others — Petya's tutors, the girls' former governess, and people who simply found it more convenient or advantageous to live at the count's expense than at home. They didn't have as many guests as before, but the old habits without which the count and countess couldn't imagine life remained unchanged. There was still the hunting establishment, which Nicholas had even expanded; the same fifty horses and fifteen grooms in the stables; the same expensive gifts and festive dinners for the whole district on name days; the count's card games of whist and boston, at which — laying out his cards so everyone could see them — he let his neighbors plunder him of hundreds of rubles a day, neighbors who considered a rubber with Count Rostov one of their most profitable sources of income.

The count moved through his affairs as through a vast net, trying not to believe he was entangled but getting more deeply caught at every step, and feeling too feeble either to tear through the mesh or to sit down and patiently untangle it. The countess, with her loving heart, sensed that her children were being ruined. It was not the count's fault — he couldn't help being what he was — and he suffered from the awareness of his own and his children's ruin, though he tried to hide it. She tried to find a remedy. From her feminine perspective, she could see only one solution: Nicholas must marry a rich heiress. She felt this was their last hope, and that if Nicholas refused the match she had found for him, she would have to give up any hope of ever setting things right. This match was with Julie Karagina, the daughter of excellent and virtuous parents, a girl the Rostovs had known since childhood and who had recently become a wealthy heiress through the death of her last surviving brother.

The countess had written directly to Julie's mother in Moscow proposing a marriage between their children and had received a favorable reply. Karagina said that for her part she was agreeable, and everything would depend on her daughter's feelings. She invited Nicholas to come to Moscow.

Several times the countess, with tears in her eyes, told her son that now both her daughters were settled, her only wish was to see him married. She said she could rest in peace if that were accomplished. Then she mentioned a wonderful girl and tried to find out what he thought about marriage.

At other times she praised Julie and urged him to go to Moscow during the holidays and enjoy himself. Nicholas guessed what his mother was driving at, and during one of these conversations he got her to speak frankly. She told him that their only hope of untangling the family's finances now lay in his marrying Julie Karagina.

"But, Mama, suppose I loved a girl who has no fortune — would you expect me to sacrifice my feelings and my honor for money?" he asked his mother, not realizing the cruelty of his question and only wanting to demonstrate his own nobility.

"No, you've misunderstood me," said his mother, not knowing how to defend herself. "You've misunderstood me, Nikolenka. It's your happiness I want," she added, feeling she was not being truthful and was getting tangled up. She began to cry.
"Mama, don't cry! Just tell me you want it, and you know I'll give my life — anything — to make you happy," said Nicholas. "I would sacrifice anything for you — even my feelings."
But the countess didn't want the question framed that way: she didn't want a sacrifice from her son — she wanted to sacrifice for him.
"No, you've misunderstood me — let's not talk about it," she said, wiping her tears.

"Maybe I do love a poor girl," Nicholas thought to himself. "Am I supposed to sacrifice my feelings and my honor for money? I wonder how Mama could say such a thing to me. Because Sonya is poor, I mustn't love her," he thought, "mustn't respond to her faithful, devoted love? And yet I'd certainly be happier with her than with some doll-like Julie. I can always sacrifice my feelings for the family's sake," he told himself, "but I can't force my feelings. If I love Sonya, that feeling is, for me, stronger and more sacred than anything."

Nicholas did not go to Moscow, and the countess did not bring up the subject of marriage again. She watched with sorrow and sometimes with anger as signs of a deepening attachment between her son and the penniless Sonya grew ever more evident. Though she blamed herself for it, she couldn't help nagging and needling Sonya, often snapping at her for no reason, addressing her coldly as "my dear" and using the formal "you" instead of the intimate "thou." The kindhearted countess was all the more vexed with Sonya because that poor, dark-eyed niece was so meek, so kind, so devotedly grateful to her benefactors, and so faithfully, unchangingly, and selflessly in love with Nicholas that there were no real grounds for finding fault with her.

Nicholas was spending the last of his leave at home. A fourth letter had arrived from Prince Andrew, this time from Rome, in which he wrote that he would have been on his way back to Russia long ago if his wound had not unexpectedly reopened in the warm climate, forcing him to postpone his return until the beginning of the new year. Natasha was still as much in love with her fiance and found the same comfort in that love, and was still as ready to throw herself into all the pleasures of life as before; but toward the end of the fourth month of their separation she began to have bouts of depression she couldn't master. She felt sorry for herself: sorry that she was being wasted all this time and was no use to anyone — while she felt herself so capable of loving and being loved.
Things were not cheerful in the Rostov household.

title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: Christmas came, and apart from the formal Mass, the solemn and tedious holiday congratulations from neighbors and servants, and the new outfits everyone wore, there were no special festivities — though the crisp frost of twenty degrees below, the dazzling sunshine by day, and the starlit winter nights seemed to call for some celebration.

On the third day of Christmas week, after the midday meal, the household dispersed to various rooms. It was the dullest time of day. Nicholas, who had been visiting neighbors that morning, was asleep on the sitting room sofa. The old count was resting in his study. Sonya sat in the drawing room at the round table, copying an embroidery pattern. The countess was playing solitaire. Nastasya Ivanovna the buffoon sat with a sad face by the window with two old ladies. Natasha came into the room, went up to Sonya, glanced at what she was doing, then went to her mother and stood there without speaking.
"Why are you wandering about like a lost soul?" asked her mother. "What do you want?"
"Him... I want him... right now, this minute! I want him!" said Natasha, her eyes glittering, without a trace of a smile.
The countess raised her head and looked at her daughter attentively.
"Don't look at me, Mama! Don't look — I'll burst into tears."
"Sit down here with me for a minute," said the countess.
"Mama, I want him. Why am I being wasted like this, Mama?"
Her voice broke, tears poured from her eyes, and she turned quickly to hide them and left the room.

She went into the sitting room, stood there thinking for a moment, and then walked into the servants' quarters. There an old maidservant was scolding a young girl who stood panting, having just run in from the cold outside.
"Stop playing around — there's a time for everything," said the old woman.
"Leave her alone, Kondratevna," said Natasha. "Go on, Mavrushka, go."
Having released Mavrushka, Natasha crossed the ballroom and went to the vestibule. There an old footman and two young ones were playing cards. They broke off and stood up when she entered.
"What can I do with them?" thought Natasha.
"Oh, Nikita, please go... where can I send him?... Yes, go to the yard and bring me a chicken — a rooster, please. And you, Misha, bring me some oats."
"Just a few oats?" said Misha, cheerfully and eagerly.
"Go, go quickly," the old man urged him.
"And you, Theodore, get me a piece of chalk."
Passing the butler's pantry on her way, she told them to set up the samovar, though it was not at all time for tea.
Foka, the butler, was the most ill-tempered person in the house. Natasha liked to test her power over him. He didn't trust the order and asked whether the samovar was really wanted.
"Oh dear, what a young lady!" said Foka, pretending to frown at Natasha.

No one in the house sent people running around or gave them as much trouble as Natasha did. She couldn't see people sitting idle without sending them off on some errand. She seemed to be testing whether any of them would get angry or sulky with her; but the servants carried out no one's orders as willingly as they did hers. "What can I do? Where can I go?" she thought, walking slowly down the corridor.
"Nastasya Ivanovna, what kind of children will I have?" she asked the buffoon, who was coming toward her in a woman's jacket.
"Why, fleas, crickets, grasshoppers," answered the buffoon.
"O Lord, O Lord, it's always the same! Oh, where am I to go? What am I to do with myself?" And tapping her heels, she ran quickly upstairs to see Vogel and his wife, who lived on the upper floor.

Two governesses were sitting with the Vogels at a table covered with plates of raisins, walnuts, and almonds. They were discussing whether it was cheaper to live in Moscow or Odessa. Natasha sat down, listened to their talk with a serious, thoughtful expression, and then got up again.

"The island of Madagascar," she said. "Ma-da-gas-car," she repeated, pronouncing each syllable distinctly, and without responding to Madame Schoss, who asked her what she was saying, she left the room.
Her brother Petya was also upstairs; with his personal attendant he was preparing fireworks to set off that night.
"Petya! Petya!" she called to him. "Carry me downstairs."
Petya ran up and offered her his back. She jumped on, throwing her arms around his neck, and he pranced along with her.
"No, stop... the island of Madagascar!" she said, and jumping off his back she went downstairs.

Having, as it were, reviewed her kingdom, tested her authority, and confirmed that everyone was obedient — yet found that it was still boring — Natasha went to the ballroom, picked up her guitar, sat down in a dark corner behind a bookcase, and began running her fingers over the bass strings, picking out a passage from an opera she had heard in Petersburg with Prince Andrew. What she produced from the guitar would have meant nothing to other listeners, but in her imagination a whole cascade of memories rose from those sounds. She sat behind the bookcase with her eyes fixed on a streak of light escaping from the pantry door and listened to herself and reflected. She was in a mood for dwelling on the past.

Sonya passed by the pantry with a glass in her hand. Natasha glanced at her and at the crack in the pantry door, and it seemed to her that she remembered the light falling through that crack once before, and Sonya passing with a glass in her hand. "Yes, it was exactly the same," thought Natasha.
"Sonya, what is this?" she called out, plucking a thick string.
"Oh, you're in here!" said Sonya with a start, and came closer to listen. "I don't know. A storm?" she ventured timidly, afraid of being wrong.
"There! That's exactly how she flinched, and how she came up smiling timidly when all this happened before," thought Natasha, "and in just the same way I thought there was something lacking in her."
"No, it's the chorus from The Water Carrier — listen!" And Natasha sang the chorus melody so Sonya could recognize it. "Where were you going?" she asked.
"To change the water in this glass. I'm just finishing the design."
"You always find something to keep you busy, but I can't," said Natasha. "And where's Nicholas?"
"Asleep, I think."
"Sonya, go wake him up," said Natasha. "Tell him I want him to come and sing."

She sat for a while, wondering what it meant that all of this had happened before, and without solving that puzzle or feeling any regret at not solving it, she let her mind drift back to the time when she was with him and he was looking at her with a lover's eyes.

"Oh, if only he would come soon! I'm so afraid it will never happen! And worst of all, I'm growing old — that's the thing! Then there won't be in me what there is now. But maybe he'll come today — come this very minute. Maybe he has already come and is sitting in the drawing room. Maybe he came yesterday and I've forgotten it." She got up, put down the guitar, and went to the drawing room.
All the household — tutors, governesses, guests — were already at the tea table. The servants stood around it. But Prince Andrew was not there, and life was going on as before.
"Ah, here she is!" said the old count when he saw Natasha come in. "Well, sit down by me." But Natasha stayed near her mother and glanced around as if looking for something.
"Mama!" she murmured. "Give him to me, give him, Mama — quickly, quickly!" and again she could barely hold back her sobs.

She sat down at the table and listened to the conversation between the elders and Nicholas, who had also come in. "My God, my God! The same faces, the same talk, Papa holding his cup and blowing the same way!" thought Natasha, feeling with horror a wave of revulsion rising in her toward the whole household, because they were always, always the same.
After tea, Nicholas, Sonya, and Natasha went to the sitting room, to their favorite corner where their most intimate conversations always took place.

title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: "Does it ever happen to you," said Natasha to her brother when they had settled down in the sitting room, "does it ever happen that you feel as if nothing more is going to come — nothing — that everything good is already past? And not exactly bored, but sad?"

"Absolutely!" he said. "I've felt that way when everything was perfectly fine and everyone was cheerful. The thought would come to me that I was already tired of it all, and that we must all die. Once in the regiment I didn't go to some party where there was music... and suddenly I felt so low..."

"Oh yes, I know, I know, I know!" Natasha interrupted. "When I was little it used to happen to me. Remember when I was punished about those plums? You were all dancing, and I sat sobbing in the schoolroom? I'll never forget it — I felt sad and sorry for everyone, for myself and for everyone. And I was innocent — that was the main thing," said Natasha. "Do you remember?"

"I remember," answered Nicholas. "I remember coming to you afterward, wanting to comfort you — but, you know, I felt ashamed. We were terribly silly. I had a funny doll then and wanted to give it to you. Do you remember?"

"And do you remember," Natasha asked with a pensive smile, "how once, long, long ago, when we were quite small, Uncle called us into the study — that was in the old house — and it was dark — we went in and suddenly there stood..."
"A Black man," chimed in Nicholas with a smile of delight. "Of course I remember. Even now I don't know whether there really was a Black man, or if we only dreamed it or were told about it."
"He was gray, remember, and had white teeth, and he stood there looking at us..."
"Sonya, do you remember?" asked Nicholas.
"Yes, yes — I remember something too," Sonya answered timidly.
"You know, I've asked Papa and Mama about that man," said Natasha, "and they say there was no one at all. But you see — you remember!"
"Of course I do — I remember his teeth as if I'd just seen them."
"How strange it is! It's like a dream. I love that."
"And do you remember how we rolled hard-boiled eggs in the ballroom, and suddenly two old women started spinning around on the carpet? Was that real or not? Do you remember how funny it was?"
"Yes, and remember how Papa in his blue overcoat fired a gun on the porch?"

So they went through their memories, smiling with pleasure — not the sad memories of old age, but poetic, youthful ones, those impressions from one's most distant past where dreams and reality blend — and they laughed with quiet contentment.
Sonya, as always, couldn't quite keep pace with them, though they shared the same memories.
Much of what they remembered had slipped from her mind, and what she did recall didn't stir the same poetic feeling they experienced. She simply enjoyed their pleasure and tried to share in it.

She only truly participated when they recalled Sonya's first arrival. She told them how afraid she had been of Nicholas because he was wearing a braided jacket and her nurse had told her she too would be sewn up with braids.
"And I remember them saying you had been born under a cabbage," said Natasha. "I remember that I didn't dare not believe it, but I knew it wasn't true, and I felt so uncomfortable."
While they were talking, a maid poked her head in through the other door of the sitting room.
"They've brought the rooster, miss," she said in a whisper.
"It's not needed, Polya. Tell them to take it away," replied Natasha.
In the middle of their conversation, Dimmler came in and walked over to the harp standing in the corner. He removed its cloth covering, and the harp gave out a jarring sound.
"Mr. Dimmler, please play my favorite nocturne by Field," came the old countess's voice from the drawing room.
Dimmler struck a chord and, turning to Natasha, Nicholas, and Sonya, remarked: "How quiet you young people are!"
"Yes, we're philosophizing," said Natasha, glancing up for a moment, then continuing the conversation. They were now discussing dreams.

Dimmler began to play; Natasha tiptoed to the table, took a candle, carried it out, and returned, seating herself quietly in her former place. It was dark in the room, especially where they sat on the sofa, but through the large windows the silvery light of the full moon fell on the floor. Dimmler finished the piece but remained at the harp, softly running his fingers over the strings, clearly undecided whether to stop or play something else.

"Do you know," said Natasha in a whisper, moving closer to Nicholas and Sonya, "that when you keep going back and back through your memories, you finally start to remember things that happened before you were even born..."
"That's metempsychosis," said Sonya, who had always been a good student and remembered everything. "The Egyptians believed that our souls once lived in animals and will return to animals again."

"No, I don't believe we were ever in animals," said Natasha, still whispering even though the music had stopped. "But I'm certain we were angels somewhere up there, and we've been here before, and that's why we remember..."
"May I join you?" said Dimmler, who had come up quietly, and he sat down with them.
"If we were angels, why have we fallen lower?" said Nicholas. "No, that can't be!"

"Not lower — who said we were lower?... How do I know what I was before?" Natasha shot back with conviction. "The soul is immortal — well then, if I shall always live, I must have lived before, lived for a whole eternity."
"Yes, but it's hard for us to imagine eternity," remarked Dimmler, who had joined the young people with a mildly patronizing smile but now spoke as quietly and seriously as they did.
"Why is it hard to imagine eternity?" said Natasha. "It's today now, and it will be tomorrow, and always; and there was yesterday, and the day before..."
"Natasha! Your turn now. Sing something for me," called the countess. "Why are you sitting there like conspirators?"
"Mama, I really don't want to," replied Natasha, but she got up all the same.

None of them — not even the middle-aged Dimmler — wanted to break off their conversation and leave that corner of the sitting room. But Natasha stood up, and Nicholas sat down at the clavichord. Standing as she always did in the middle of the hall, choosing the spot with the best acoustics, Natasha began to sing her mother's favorite song.

She had said she didn't want to sing, but it had been a long time since she had sung, and a long time before she would sing again as she did that evening. The count, from his study where he was talking with Mitenka, heard her — and like a schoolboy rushing out to play, he stumbled over his words while giving orders to the steward and finally stopped, while Mitenka stood before him also listening and smiling. Nicholas didn't take his eyes off his sister and drew breath in time with her. Sonya, listening, thought of the vast difference between herself and her friend and how impossible it was for her to be anything like as captivating as her cousin. The old countess sat with a blissful yet sad smile and tears in her eyes, shaking her head now and then. She was thinking about Natasha and about her own youth, and about how there was something unnatural and frightening in this approaching marriage of Natasha and Prince Andrew.
Dimmler, who had seated himself beside the countess, listened with closed eyes.
"Ah, Countess," he said at last, "that is a European talent — she has nothing to learn. What softness, tenderness, and strength..."

"Ah, how afraid I am for her, how afraid!" said the countess, not realizing whom she was speaking to. Her maternal instinct told her that there was too much of something in Natasha and that because of this she would not be happy. Before Natasha had finished singing, fourteen-year-old Petya burst in excitedly to announce that mummers had arrived.
Natasha stopped abruptly.
"Idiot!" she screamed at her brother and, running to a chair, threw herself into it, sobbing so violently that she couldn't stop for a long time.
"It's nothing, Mama, really nothing — Petya just startled me," she said, trying to smile, but tears kept flowing and sobs still shook her.

The mummers — house serfs dressed up as bears, Turks, innkeepers, and fine ladies — frightening and funny, bringing with them the cold from outside and a feeling of gaiety, crowded at first timidly into the anteroom, then, hiding behind one another, pushed into the ballroom where, shyly at first and then more and more merrily and wholeheartedly, they began singing, dancing, and playing Christmas games. The countess, after identifying them and laughing at their costumes, went into the drawing room. The count sat in the ballroom, beaming and applauding. The young people had vanished.

Half an hour later there appeared among the other mummers: an old lady in a hooped skirt — Nicholas; a Turkish girl — Petya; a clown — Dimmler; a hussar — Natasha; and a Circassian — Sonya, with mustache and eyebrows drawn in burnt cork.

After the condescending surprise, the failure to recognize anyone, and the praise from the people who were not in costume, the young people decided that their outfits were so good they needed to be shown elsewhere.
Nicholas, who was eager to take them all for a ride in his troika since the roads were in splendid condition, proposed to bring about a dozen of the serf mummers and drive to "Uncle's."
"No, why bother the old fellow?" said the countess. "Besides, you wouldn't have room to turn around there. If you must go, go to the Melyukovs'."
Melyukova was a widow who lived with her family and their tutors and governesses three miles from the Rostovs.
"That's right, my dear," chimed in the old count, thoroughly enthused. "I'll dress up right away and go with them. I'll make Pashette's eyes pop."

But the countess wouldn't agree to his going; he'd had a bad leg for days. It was decided that the count must stay, but that if Louisa Ivanovna — Madame Schoss — would go with them, the young ladies could go to the Melyukovs'. Sonya, usually so timid and shy, begged Louisa Ivanovna more urgently than anyone not to refuse.

Sonya's costume was the best of all. Her mustache and eyebrows were extraordinarily becoming. Everyone said she looked very handsome, and she was in a spirited, energetic mood quite unlike her usual self. Some inner voice told her that tonight or never her fate would be decided, and in her male attire she seemed a completely different person. Louisa Ivanovna agreed to come, and within half an hour four troikas with large and small bells, their runners squeaking and whistling over the frozen snow, pulled up to the porch.

Natasha was the first to set the merry holiday mood, and this merriment, passing from one person to the next, grew stronger until it reached its peak when they all came out into the frost and got into the sleighs, talking, calling to one another, laughing, and shouting.

Two of the troikas were ordinary household sleighs; the third was the old count's, drawn by a trotter from the Orlov stud; the fourth was Nicholas's own, with a shaggy little black shaft horse. Nicholas, in his old-lady costume belted with a hussar overcoat, stood in the middle of his sleigh, reins in hand.

It was so light that he could see the moonlight reflected off the metal harness disks and off the eyes of the horses, who looked around nervously at the noisy party gathered under the shadow of the porch roof.
Natasha, Sonya, Madame Schoss, and two maids got into Nicholas's sleigh; Dimmler, his wife, and Petya into the old count's; and the rest of the mummers took the other two sleighs.
"You go first, Zakhar!" Nicholas shouted to his father's coachman, hoping for a chance to race past him.

The old count's troika, carrying Dimmler and his party, started forward with a squeak of runners as if freezing to the snow, its deep-toned bell clanging. The side horses, pressing against the shafts, sank into the dry, diamond-glinting snow and tossed it up.

Nicholas set off behind the first sleigh; behind him the others followed noisily, their runners squeaking. At first they drove at a steady trot along the narrow road. While they passed the garden the shadows of bare trees fell across the road, hiding the brilliant moonlight, but as soon as they were past the fence the snowy plain — bathed in moonlight and motionless — stretched out before them, glittering like diamonds and mottled with bluish shadows. Bang, bang! went the first sleigh over a rut in the frozen road, and each sleigh behind it jolted the same way, and rudely breaking the frost-bound stillness, the troikas began to fly along one after another.
"A hare's track — lots of tracks!" rang out Natasha's voice through the frost-bound air.
"How bright it is, Nicholas!" came Sonya's voice.

Nicholas glanced around at Sonya and bent down to see her face more closely. A quite new, sweet face with black eyebrows and a mustache peeked up at him from her sable fur — so close and yet so far away in the moonlight.
"That used to be Sonya," thought he, and looked at her more closely and smiled.
"What is it, Nicholas?"
"Nothing," he said, and turned back to the horses.

When they reached the beaten highway — polished by sleigh runners and rutted by rough-shod hooves, the marks of which shone in the moonlight — the horses began pulling at the reins of their own accord and picked up speed. The near horse arched its head, broke into a short canter, and tugged at its traces. The shaft horse swayed from side to side, flicking its ears as if asking: "Isn't it time to begin?" Ahead, already far in front, the deep bell of the lead sleigh rang out more and more distantly, and the black horses driven by Zakhar were clearly visible against the white snow. From that sleigh came shouts, laughter, and the mummers' voices.
"Gee up, my darlings!" shouted Nicholas, pulling the reins to one side and cracking the whip.

Only the sharper wind meeting them and the jerking of the side horses — pulling ever harder and quickening their gallop — showed how fast the troika was flying. Nicholas looked back. With screams, squeals, and cracking whips that sent even the shaft horses into a gallop, the other sleighs followed. The shaft horse swung steadily under the arch over its head, never thinking of slowing down, ready to put on more speed when asked.
Nicholas overtook the first sleigh. They were racing downhill and out across a broad, well-trodden track through a meadow near the river.

"Where are we?" he thought. "It must be the Kosoy meadow. But no — this is something I've never seen before. This isn't the Kosoy meadow or the Demkin hill, and heaven only knows what it is! It's something new and enchanted. Well, whatever it may be..." And shouting to his horses, he began to pass the first sleigh.
Zakhar held back his horses and turned his face — already covered with frost up to his eyebrows — toward them.
Nicholas gave his horses their head, and Zakhar, stretching out his arms, clicked his tongue and let his horses go.
"Now watch yourself, master!" he cried.

Faster and faster the two troikas flew side by side, and faster moved the galloping legs of the side horses. Nicholas began to pull ahead. Zakhar, keeping his arms stretched out, raised one hand with the reins.
"Not a chance, master!" he shouted.

Nicholas pushed all his horses into a gallop and flew past Zakhar. The horses sprayed the fine, dry snow into the faces of those in the sleigh — beside them sounded the quick jingling of bells, and they caught confused glimpses of swiftly moving legs and the shadow of the troika they were overtaking. The whistling of runners on snow and the shrieks of girls could be heard from different sides.
Checking his horses again, Nicholas looked around. They were still surrounded by the magic plain bathed in moonlight and spangled with stars.

"Zakhar is shouting that I should turn left — but why left?" thought Nicholas. "Are we getting to the Melyukovs'? Is this Melyukovka? Heaven only knows where we're going, and heaven knows what's happening to us — but it's very strange and wonderful, whatever it is." And he looked around in the sleigh.
"Look — his mustache and eyelashes are all white!" said one of the strange, pretty, unfamiliar people — the one with the fine eyebrows and mustache.
"I think this used to be Natasha," thought Nicholas, "and that was Madame Schoss — but maybe not. And this Circassian with the mustache I don't know, but I love her."
"Aren't you cold?" he asked.
They didn't answer but started laughing. Dimmler shouted something from the sleigh behind — probably something funny — but they couldn't make out what he said.
"Yes, yes!" some voices answered, laughing.

"But here was a fairy forest with black moving shadows and a glitter of diamonds and a flight of marble steps and the silver roofs of fairy buildings and the shrill cries of strange creatures. And if this really is Melyukovka, it is stranger still that we drove heaven knows where and have arrived at Melyukovka," thought Nicholas.
It really was Melyukovka, and maids and footmen with merry faces came running out onto the porch carrying candles.
"Who is it?" asked someone from the porch.
"The mummers from the count's. I know by the horses," replied several voices.

title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: Pelageya Danilovna Melyukova, a broadly built, energetic woman in spectacles, sat in the drawing room in a loose dress, surrounded by her daughters whom she was trying to keep from getting bored. They were quietly pouring melted wax into snow and looking at the shadow shapes the wax figures would cast on the wall, when they heard the steps and voices of new arrivals in the vestibule.

Hussars, ladies, witches, clowns, and bears — after clearing their throats and wiping the frost from their faces in the vestibule — came into the ballroom, where candles were hastily lit. The clown, Dimmler, and the lady, Nicholas, started a dance. Surrounded by screaming children, the mummers — covering their faces and disguising their voices — bowed to their hostess and spread out around the room.

"Goodness, I can't tell who's who! And Natasha! See who she looks like! She really does remind me of someone. But Herr Dimmler — isn't he wonderful! I never recognized him! And the way he dances! Heavens, there's a Circassian. Really, how becoming it is on dear Sonya. And who is that? Well, you've certainly cheered us up! Nikita and Vanya — clear the tables! And we were sitting here so quietly. Ha, ha, ha!... The hussar — the hussar! Just like a boy! And the legs!... I can't look at him..." Different voices rang out.

Natasha, the young Melyukovs' favorite, disappeared with them into the back rooms where cork and various dressing gowns and men's clothes were requested and received from the footman through a door by bare girlish arms. Ten minutes later all the young Melyukovs had joined the mummers.

Pelageya Danilovna, having given orders to clear the rooms and arrange refreshments for both the gentry and the servants, walked among the mummers without removing her spectacles, peering into their faces with a suppressed smile and failing to recognize any of them. It wasn't only Dimmler and the Rostovs she couldn't identify — she didn't even recognize her own daughters, or her late husband's dressing gowns and uniforms, which they had put on.

"And who is this?" she asked her governess, peering into the face of her own daughter dressed as a Kazan Tartar. "I think it must be one of the Rostovs! Well, Mr. Hussar, which regiment do you serve in?" she asked Natasha. "Here, pass some fruit jelly to the Turk!" she told the butler who was serving. "His religion doesn't forbid it."

Sometimes, watching the strange but amusing antics of the dancers — who, having once decided that no one could recognize them in disguise, were not shy at all — Pelageya Danilovna hid her face in her handkerchief, and her whole stout body shook with irrepressible, kindly, elderly laughter.
"My little Sasha! Look at Sasha!" she said.

After Russian country dances and round dances, Pelageya Danilovna made everyone — serfs and gentry alike — form one big circle: a ring, a string, and a silver ruble were fetched, and they all played games together.

Within an hour, all the costumes were rumpled and disordered. The corked eyebrows and mustaches were smeared over perspiring, flushed, and merry faces. Pelageya Danilovna began to recognize people, admired their cleverly contrived costumes — particularly how well they suited the young ladies — and thanked them all for being so entertaining. The guests were invited to supper in the drawing room, and the servants were served something in the ballroom.
"Now, telling one's fortune in the empty bathhouse — that's frightening!" said an old maid who lived with the Melyukovs, during supper.
"Why?" asked the eldest Melyukov girl.
"You wouldn't go. It takes courage..."
"I'll go," said Sonya.
"Tell what happened to the young lady!" said the second Melyukov girl.

"Well," began the old maid, "a young lady once went out, took a rooster, laid a table for two — all proper — and sat down. After sitting a while, she suddenly hears someone coming... a sleigh pulls up with harness bells; she hears him arrive! He comes in, looking just like a man — an officer — and sits down at the table with her."
"Aah! Aah!" screamed Natasha, her eyes round with horror.
"Yes? And how... did he speak?"

"Yes, just like a man. Everything perfectly normal. And he started trying to convince her about things, and she was supposed to keep him talking till the cock crowed. But she got frightened — just got frightened and hid her face in her hands. And he grabbed her. It was lucky the maids ran in just then..."
"Now, why scare them?" said Pelageya Danilovna.
"Mama, you used to try your own fortune..." said her daughter.
"And how does one do it in a barn?" asked Sonya.
"Well, say you went to the barn now and listened. It depends on what you hear: hammering and knocking — that's bad; but the sound of shifting grain is good, and sometimes one does hear that."
"Mama, tell us what happened to you in the barn."
Pelageya Danilovna smiled.
"Oh, I've forgotten..." she said. "But none of you would go, would you?"
"Yes, I will; Pelageya Danilovna, let me! I'll go," said Sonya.
"All right, why not — if you're not afraid?"
"Louisa Ivanovna, may I?" asked Sonya.

Whether they were playing the ring-and-string game or the ruble game or talking as they were now, Nicholas never left Sonya's side and looked at her with completely new eyes. It seemed to him that it was only today, thanks to that burnt-cork mustache, that he had truly seen her for the first time. And really, that evening Sonya was brighter, livelier, and prettier than Nicholas had ever seen her before.

"So that's what she's like — what a fool I've been!" he thought, gazing at her sparkling eyes and the happy, rapturous smile that dimpled her cheeks beneath the mustache — a smile he had never seen before.
"I'm not afraid of anything," said Sonya. "May I go right now?" She stood up.
They told her where the barn was and how to stand and listen, and handed her a fur cloak. She threw it over her head and shoulders and glanced at Nicholas.
"What a darling girl she is!" he thought. "And what have I been thinking all this time?"
Sonya went out into the passage toward the barn. Nicholas hurried to the front porch, saying he was too hot. The crowd of people really had made the house stuffy.

Outside there was the same cold stillness and the same moon, only brighter than before. The light was so strong and the snow sparkled with so many stars that one didn't want to look up at the sky — the real stars went unnoticed. The sky was black and somber, while the earth was gay.

"I am a fool, a fool! What have I been waiting for?" thought Nicholas, and running off the porch he went around the corner of the house and along the path to the back porch. He knew Sonya would come this way. Halfway along lay some snow-covered piles of firewood, and across and along them a web of shadows from the bare old linden trees fell on the snow and on the path. This path led to the barn. The log walls of the barn and its snow-covered roof, which looked as if carved from some precious stone, sparkled in the moonlight. A tree cracked in the garden from the frost, and then everything was perfectly silent again. His chest seemed to inhale not air but the strength of eternal youth and gladness.

From the back porch came the sound of feet descending the steps; the bottom step, on which snow had fallen, gave a ringing creak, and he heard an old maidservant's voice saying: "Straight on, straight along the path, miss. Only, don't look back."
"I'm not afraid," answered Sonya's voice, and along the path toward Nicholas came the crunching, whistling sound of Sonya's feet in her thin shoes.

Sonya came along, wrapped in her cloak. She was only a couple of steps away when she saw him — and to her too he was not the Nicholas she had always known and slightly feared. He was in a woman's dress, with tousled hair and a happy smile new to Sonya. She ran quickly toward him.

"Completely different and yet the same," thought Nicholas, looking at her face, all lit up by the moonlight. He slipped his arms under the cloak that covered her head, embraced her, drew her close, and kissed her on the lips that wore a mustache and smelled of burnt cork.
